Part C — CBAM-Enhanced CNN for EMNIST Letters¶

1. Introduction¶

1.1 Background¶

In CA1 Part A, three CNN versions were developed for EMNIST Letters classification:

  • V1: baseline CNN
  • V2: deeper CNN with Batch Normalisation and Dropout
  • V3: the V2 architecture trained with realistic data augmentation

The CA1 experiments showed that deeper feature extraction, regularisation and data augmentation improved overall classification performance. V3 achieved the strongest overall result, but confusion remained between visually similar handwritten letters, particularly I and L.

This Part C experiment investigates the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) as an advanced extension to the CA1 CNN architecture.

CBAM sequentially applies two attention mechanisms:

  • Channel Attention Module (CAM): learns what feature channels contain important information
  • Spatial Attention Module (SAM): learns where important information is located within the feature maps

Rather than assuming that CBAM will always improve performance, this experiment evaluates how much benefit it provides when added to both the V2 and V3 configurations.

1.2 Research Question¶

  1. To what extent does integrating CBAM improve CNN-based EMNIST Letters classification, particularly for the visually ambiguous I and L classes?

  2. Does CBAM remain beneficial when combined with the stronger CA1 V3 data-augmentation strategy?

1.3 Experimental Approach¶

The notebook keeps the following settings consistent where applicable:

Setting Value
Dataset EMNIST Letters
Preprocessing Same cleaning and preprocessing as CA1
Data split 70% / 15% / 15% (train / validation / test)
Random seed 88
Backbone V2 / V3 CNN
Optimiser Adam, learning rate 0.0005
Loss Categorical cross-entropy
Batch size 128
Max epochs 20
Early stopping Based on validation loss

Two controlled comparisons are performed:

  1. Experiment 1: V2 Baseline vs V2 + CBAM
  2. Experiment 2: V3 Augmented vs V3 + CBAM

For Experiment 1, the V2 CNN is compared with the same architecture enhanced using CBAM. This isolates the effect of the attention mechanism without introducing data augmentation.

For Experiment 2, both models use the same V3 augmentation configuration, so CBAM remains the main architectural difference.

The models are evaluated using:

  • test accuracy
  • test loss
  • macro F1-score
  • I and L precision and recall
  • I→L and L→I errors
  • total I↔L confusion
  • parameter count
  • training time

4. Data Cleaning¶

Purpose

The raw CSV contains invalid labels and duplicate rows. The same cleaning steps used in CA1 Part A are repeated before model training.

Cleaning Steps

  1. Keep only labels from 1 to 26.
  2. Remove duplicated rows.
  3. Separate the labels and image pixels.
  4. Convert labels from 1–26 to 0–25.

This section is kept concise because the detailed data-quality investigation was already completed in CA1 Part A.

In [16]:
# Keep only valid labels 1–26
mask = (data.iloc[:, 0] >= 1) & (data.iloc[:, 0] <= 26)
data = data[mask].copy()

print("After label cleaning:", data.shape)

# Remove duplicate rows
data = data.drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)

print("After removing duplicates:", data.shape)

# Separate labels and pixels
y_int = data.iloc[:, 0].to_numpy().astype("int32") - 1
X = data.iloc[:, 1:].to_numpy().astype("float32")

print("Label range:", y_int.min(), "to", y_int.max())
print("Pixel range:", X.min(), "to", X.max())

5. Image Reshaping, Orientation Correction and Normalisation¶

Purpose

CNNs require image-shaped inputs rather than flat 784-element vectors.

The preprocessing follows CA1 Part A:

  • reshape each sample to 28×28;
  • transpose each image to correct the EMNIST orientation;
  • add a single grayscale channel;
  • normalise pixel values from 0–255 to 0–1.

No additional horizontal flip is applied.

In [17]:
# Reshape flat vectors into 28×28 images
X = X.reshape(-1, 28, 28)

# Correct EMNIST orientation
X = np.transpose(X, (0, 2, 1))

# Add grayscale channel dimension
X = X[..., np.newaxis]

# Normalise pixel values
X = X.astype("float32") / 255.0

print("Processed X shape:", X.shape)
print("Pixel range:", X.min(), "to", X.max())

7. Experiment 1 — V2 Baseline vs V2 + CBAM¶

7.1 Control Model — CA1 V2 CNN¶

Purpose

The V2 CNN is used as the control model because it already contains the main architectural improvements from CA1:

  • three convolutional layers;
  • Batch Normalisation;
  • Max Pooling;
  • a 256-neuron dense layer;
  • Dropout.

V2 is preferred over V3 for this experiment because V3 introduces data augmentation. Using V2 makes it easier to isolate the effect of CBAM.

V2 Architecture

  • Conv2D 32 → BatchNorm → MaxPool
  • Conv2D 64 → BatchNorm → MaxPool
  • Conv2D 128 → BatchNorm
  • Flatten → Dense 256 → Dropout 0.4 → Softmax
In [20]:
def build_v2_baseline(input_shape=(28, 28, 1), num_classes=26):
    inputs = Input(shape=input_shape, name="input")

    x = Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation="relu", name="conv1")(inputs)
    x = BatchNormalization(name="bn1")(x)
    x = MaxPooling2D((2, 2), name="pool1")(x)

    x = Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation="relu", padding="same", name="conv2")(x)
    x = BatchNormalization(name="bn2")(x)
    x = MaxPooling2D((2, 2), name="pool2")(x)

    x = Conv2D(128, (3, 3), activation="relu", padding="same", name="conv3")(x)
    x = BatchNormalization(name="bn3")(x)

    x = Flatten(name="flatten")(x)
    x = Dense(256, activation="relu", name="dense256")(x)
    x = Dropout(0.4, name="dropout")(x)

    outputs = Dense(num_classes, activation="softmax", name="output")(x)

    return Model(inputs, outputs, name="CA1_V2_Baseline")


baseline_model = build_v2_baseline()

baseline_model.compile(
    loss="categorical_crossentropy",
    optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.0005),
    metrics=["accuracy"]
)

baseline_model.summary()

7.2 Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM)¶

CBAM is the advanced CNN component investigated in Part C.

It applies two attention stages sequentially:

  1. Channel Attention Module (CAM) — determines which feature channels are more useful.
  2. Spatial Attention Module (SAM) — determines which locations in the feature map are more useful.

Channel Attention Module¶

CAM uses global average pooling and global max pooling to summarise each feature channel. The two descriptors pass through a shared small multilayer perceptron and a sigmoid function.

The result is a set of channel-wise weights that strengthens useful feature maps and suppresses less useful ones.

Spatial Attention Module¶

SAM pools the channel-refined tensor across the channel dimension using average and maximum values. The two spatial maps are concatenated and passed through a 7×7 convolution.

The result is a 2-D attention map that highlights more informative locations.

In [21]:
def channel_attention(inputs, reduction_ratio=8, name="cam"):
    channels = int(inputs.shape[-1])
    hidden_units = max(channels // reduction_ratio, 1)

    avg_pool = GlobalAveragePooling2D(name=f"{name}_gap")(inputs)
    max_pool = GlobalMaxPooling2D(name=f"{name}_gmp")(inputs)

    shared_dense_1 = Dense(
        hidden_units,
        activation="relu",
        use_bias=True,
        name=f"{name}_mlp1"
    )

    shared_dense_2 = Dense(
        channels,
        use_bias=True,
        name=f"{name}_mlp2"
    )

    avg_out = shared_dense_2(shared_dense_1(avg_pool))
    max_out = shared_dense_2(shared_dense_1(max_pool))

    attention = Add(name=f"{name}_add")([avg_out, max_out])
    attention = Activation("sigmoid", name=f"{name}_sigmoid")(attention)
    attention = Reshape((1, 1, channels), name=f"{name}_reshape")(attention)

    return Multiply(name=f"{name}_scale")([inputs, attention])


def spatial_attention(inputs, kernel_size=7, name="sam"):
    avg_pool = tf.reduce_mean(inputs, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    max_pool = tf.reduce_max(inputs, axis=-1, keepdims=True)

    x = Concatenate(axis=-1, name=f"{name}_concat")([avg_pool, max_pool])

    attention = Conv2D(
        1,
        kernel_size,
        padding="same",
        activation="sigmoid",
        use_bias=False,
        name=f"{name}_conv"
    )(x)

    return Multiply(name=f"{name}_scale")([inputs, attention])


def cbam_block(inputs, reduction_ratio=8, spatial_kernel=7, name="cbam"):
    x = channel_attention(
        inputs,
        reduction_ratio=reduction_ratio,
        name=f"{name}_cam"
    )

    x = spatial_attention(
        x,
        kernel_size=spatial_kernel,
        name=f"{name}_sam"
    )

    return x

7.3 Advanced Model — V2 CNN + CBAM¶

Hypothesis

Adding CBAM may improve feature selection by helping the model emphasise important channels and local spatial details.

For I and L, this may help the model focus on small structural differences such as a short base stroke or endpoint.

This is a hypothesis only. The experiment must determine whether CBAM actually improves the results.

Model Design

The V2 backbone is kept unchanged as much as possible.

CBAM is inserted:

  • after the first BatchNorm layer;
  • after the second BatchNorm layer;
  • after the third BatchNorm layer.

Therefore, the main experimental change is the addition of attention.

In [22]:
def build_v2_cbam(input_shape=(28, 28, 1), num_classes=26, reduction_ratio=8):
    inputs = Input(shape=input_shape, name="input")

    x = Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation="relu", name="conv1")(inputs)
    x = BatchNormalization(name="bn1")(x)
    x = cbam_block(x, reduction_ratio=reduction_ratio, name="cbam1")
    x = MaxPooling2D((2, 2), name="pool1")(x)

    x = Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation="relu", padding="same", name="conv2")(x)
    x = BatchNormalization(name="bn2")(x)
    x = cbam_block(x, reduction_ratio=reduction_ratio, name="cbam2")
    x = MaxPooling2D((2, 2), name="pool2")(x)

    x = Conv2D(128, (3, 3), activation="relu", padding="same", name="conv3")(x)
    x = BatchNormalization(name="bn3")(x)
    x = cbam_block(x, reduction_ratio=reduction_ratio, name="cbam3")

    x = Flatten(name="flatten")(x)
    x = Dense(256, activation="relu", name="dense256")(x)
    x = Dropout(0.4, name="dropout")(x)

    outputs = Dense(num_classes, activation="softmax", name="output")(x)

    return Model(inputs, outputs, name="CA1_V2_CBAM")


cbam_model = build_v2_cbam()

cbam_model.compile(
    loss="categorical_crossentropy",
    optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.0005),
    metrics=["accuracy"]
)

cbam_model.summary()

7.4 Parameter Comparison¶

Before training, the parameter counts are compared to measure the additional model complexity introduced by CBAM.

In [23]:
baseline_params = baseline_model.count_params()
cbam_params = cbam_model.count_params()

parameter_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Model": ["V2 Baseline", "V2 + CBAM"],
    "Parameters": [baseline_params, cbam_params]
})

display(parameter_table)

param_increase = cbam_params - baseline_params
param_increase_pct = (param_increase / baseline_params) * 100

print(f"Additional parameters from CBAM: {param_increase:,}")
print(f"Relative parameter increase: {param_increase_pct:.3f}%")
Model Parameters
0 V2 Baseline 1280154
1 V2 + CBAM 1286076 
Additional parameters from CBAM: 5,922
Relative parameter increase: 0.463%

Parameter Comparison Analysis¶

Adding CBAM increased the model size only slightly.

  • The V2 Baseline contains 1,280,154 parameters.
  • The V2 + CBAM model contains 1,286,076 parameters.
  • CBAM therefore adds only 5,922 parameters, which is a relative increase of approximately 0.463%.

This shows that CBAM is lightweight in terms of parameter count. The attention mechanism adds channel and spatial recalibration without substantially increasing the number of trainable parameters.

Therefore, any later performance improvement can be evaluated against a relatively small increase in model size. However, parameter count alone does not represent total computational cost, so the training-time comparison is also considered later.

7.5 Training Setup¶

To isolate the effect of CBAM, both models use the same training settings:

  • loss: categorical cross-entropy;
  • optimiser: Adam;
  • learning rate: 0.0005;
  • batch size: 128;
  • maximum epochs: 20;
  • EarlyStopping monitor: validation loss;
  • patience: 4;
  • restore best weights: enabled;
  • random seed: 88.

No data augmentation is used in this primary comparison.

In [24]:
def make_early_stopping():
    return EarlyStopping(
        monitor="val_loss",
        patience=4,
        restore_best_weights=True
    )


def reset_seed(seed=SEED):
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    tf.random.set_seed(seed)

7.8 Training History Comparison¶

The training and validation curves are compared to examine:

  • convergence behaviour;
  • validation performance;
  • possible overfitting;
  • whether CBAM changes training stability.
In [27]:
def plot_history_comparison(history_a, history_b, metric="accuracy"):
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))

    plt.plot(history_a.history[metric], label=f"V2 Baseline Train")
    plt.plot(history_a.history[f"val_{metric}"], label=f"V2 Baseline Validation")
    plt.plot(history_b.history[metric], label=f"V2 + CBAM Train")
    plt.plot(history_b.history[f"val_{metric}"], label=f"V2 + CBAM Validation")

    plt.xlabel("Epoch")
    plt.ylabel(metric.title())
    plt.title(f"{metric.title()} Comparison")
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(alpha=0.3)
    plt.show()


plot_history_comparison(history_baseline, history_cbam, metric="accuracy")
plot_history_comparison(history_baseline, history_cbam, metric="loss")

Training History Analysis¶

Both models converged quickly, but the CBAM model required more training time and one additional epoch before Early Stopping.

  • The V2 baseline stopped after 7 epochs and required approximately 260.66 seconds.
  • The V2 + CBAM model stopped after 8 epochs and required approximately 640.28 seconds.

For both models, training accuracy continued to increase while validation accuracy stabilised around 93–94%.

The CBAM model achieved slightly higher validation accuracy during the middle epochs, reaching approximately 93.78% at epoch 5. However, its validation loss stopped improving after epoch 4 and later increased while training loss continued to decrease.

This indicates mild overfitting in both models, with the CBAM model showing a larger gap between training and validation loss near the end of training.

The CBAM model also required substantially longer training time despite increasing the parameter count by only 0.463%. This suggests that the attention operations add computational cost beyond what is reflected by parameter count alone.

Overall, the training curves do not yet provide clear evidence that CBAM improves generalisation. The final test-set results and I–L confusion analysis are therefore needed before determining whether the added attention mechanism is beneficial.

7.9 Test-Set Evaluation¶

Evaluation Metrics

Overall accuracy alone is not enough because CA1 showed that improved overall performance could still leave I–L confusion unresolved.

The experiment therefore evaluates:

  • test accuracy;
  • test loss;
  • macro F1-score;
  • precision and recall for I;
  • precision and recall for L;
  • I→L errors;
  • L→I errors;
  • total I↔L confusion;
  • parameter count;
  • training time.
In [28]:
LETTERS = np.array(list(string.ascii_uppercase))
I_INDEX = 8
L_INDEX = 11


def evaluate_model(model, model_name, training_time):
    test_loss, test_accuracy = model.evaluate(X_test, y_test, verbose=0)

    probabilities = model.predict(X_test, verbose=0)
    y_pred = np.argmax(probabilities, axis=1)

    macro_f1 = f1_score(y_test_int, y_pred, average="macro")

    cm = confusion_matrix(
        y_test_int,
        y_pred,
        labels=np.arange(NUM_CLASSES)
    )

    i_to_l = int(cm[I_INDEX, L_INDEX])
    l_to_i = int(cm[L_INDEX, I_INDEX])

    return {
        "Model": model_name,
        "Test Accuracy (%)": test_accuracy * 100,
        "Test Loss": test_loss,
        "Macro F1": macro_f1,
        "I Precision": precision_score(
            y_test_int == I_INDEX, y_pred == I_INDEX, zero_division=0
        ),
        "I Recall": recall_score(
            y_test_int == I_INDEX, y_pred == I_INDEX, zero_division=0
        ),
        "L Precision": precision_score(
            y_test_int == L_INDEX, y_pred == L_INDEX, zero_division=0
        ),
        "L Recall": recall_score(
            y_test_int == L_INDEX, y_pred == L_INDEX, zero_division=0
        ),
        "I→L Errors": i_to_l,
        "L→I Errors": l_to_i,
        "Total I↔L Errors": i_to_l + l_to_i,
        "Parameters": model.count_params(),
        "Training Time (s)": training_time,
        "Predictions": y_pred,
        "Confusion Matrix": cm
    }


baseline_result = evaluate_model(
    baseline_model,
    "V2 Baseline",
    baseline_time
)

cbam_result = evaluate_model(
    cbam_model,
    "V2 + CBAM",
    cbam_time
)

Key Observations¶

  • Overall performance remained very similar, but accuracy and macro F1 decreased slightly after adding CBAM.
  • CBAM improved L recall and reduced L→I errors, but this was offset by lower I recall and more I→L errors.
  • Total I–L confusion improved by only 1 error, from 217 to 216, so CBAM mainly redistributed the errors rather than resolving the confusion.
  • The parameter increase was very small at about 0.46%, but the observed training time increased substantially.
  • Overall, CBAM produced a class-dependent trade-off rather than a clear overall improvement.

Class-Level Performance Analysis¶

The classification reports show that the V2 Baseline and V2 + CBAM models achieved very similar performance across the 26 EMNIST classes. However, CBAM did not improve the overall classification metrics in this run.

Overall Performance¶

Metric V2 Baseline V2 + CBAM Change
Accuracy 93.95% 93.80% -0.15 percentage points
Macro Precision 0.9402 0.9382 -0.0020
Macro Recall 0.9395 0.9380 -0.0015
Macro F1 0.9392 0.9379 -0.0013
Weighted F1 0.9392 0.9379 -0.0013

Overall performance therefore remained close, but the CBAM model performed slightly worse on accuracy and F1-score.

I–L Performance¶

Class Metric V2 Baseline V2 + CBAM Change
I Precision 0.7232 0.7500 +0.0268
I Recall 0.8541 0.7879 -0.0662
I F1 0.7832 0.7685 -0.0147
L Precision 0.8269 0.7748 -0.0521
L Recall 0.6719 0.7461 +0.0742
L F1 0.7414 0.7602 +0.0188

Key observations:

  • For I, precision improved from 0.7232 to 0.7500, indicating that predictions labelled as I became slightly more reliable.
  • However, I recall decreased from 0.8541 to 0.7879, meaning that fewer true I samples were correctly recognised.
  • As a result, I F1 decreased from 0.7832 to 0.7685.
  • For L, recall improved substantially from 0.6719 to 0.7461.
  • Although L precision decreased from 0.8269 to 0.7748, its F1-score improved from 0.7414 to 0.7602.

The I–L results therefore show a clear trade-off. CBAM improved recognition of L, but this was accompanied by weaker recognition of I.

Secondary G–Q Performance¶

G and Q were also among the more difficult classes in the baseline model.

Class Metric V2 Baseline V2 + CBAM Change
G Precision 0.8634 0.8535 -0.0099
G Recall 0.8583 0.8602 +0.0019
G F1 0.8608 0.8569 -0.0039
Q Precision 0.9076 0.9019 -0.0057
Q Recall 0.8388 0.8388 0.0000
Q F1 0.8718 0.8692 -0.0026

Key observations:

  • G recall increased only slightly from 0.8583 to 0.8602.
  • The decrease in G precision caused its F1-score to fall slightly from 0.8608 to 0.8569.
  • Q recall remained unchanged at 0.8388.
  • Q precision and F1 both decreased slightly.
  • CBAM therefore provided no meaningful improvement for the G–Q pair.

Other Class-Level Changes¶

Most other classes remained strong, with F1-scores generally above 0.90.

Some notable improvements after adding CBAM include:

  • J: F1 increased from 0.9277 to 0.9469
  • S: F1 increased from 0.9738 to 0.9854
  • W: F1 increased from 0.9766 to 0.9812
  • T: F1 increased from 0.9579 to 0.9630

However, some classes decreased:

  • F: 0.9753 → 0.9626
  • H: 0.9523 → 0.9442
  • X: 0.9817 → 0.9738
  • D: 0.9521 → 0.9464

This further shows that CBAM affected individual classes differently rather than producing a consistent improvement across all letters.

Overall Interpretation¶

The class-level results show that CBAM had a class-dependent effect.

Although overall accuracy and macro F1 decreased slightly, some individual classes improved. The clearest change occurred for the difficult I–L pair: L recall and F1 improved, while I recall and F1 decreased.

For the secondary difficult pair G–Q, performance remained almost unchanged, with small decreases in F1-score.

Overall, CBAM did not provide a clear improvement across all 26 classes. Instead, it altered the balance of predictions between particular classes.

The next analysis therefore focuses on the I→L and L→I confusion directions to determine whether CBAM reduced or mainly redistributed the errors between these two visually similar letters.

7.12 I–L Confusion Comparison¶

The central motivation for this Part C experiment is the persistent confusion between I and L.

This chart compares the directional and total I–L errors directly.

I–L Confusion Analysis¶

The I–L comparison shows that CBAM changed the direction of the confusion more than it reduced the total number of errors.

Error Type V2 Baseline V2 + CBAM Change
I→L 62 95 +33
L→I 155 121 -34
Total I↔L 217 216 -1

Key Observations¶

  • I→L errors increased from 62 to 95, meaning that more true I samples were misclassified as L after adding CBAM.
  • L→I errors decreased from 155 to 121, showing that CBAM improved the model's ability to recognise L instead of predicting I.
  • These two changes almost completely offset each other.
  • Total I↔L confusion decreased by only 1 error, from 217 to 216.

Interpretation¶

CBAM therefore did not substantially resolve the I–L confusion. Instead, it mainly redistributed the errors between the two directions.

This is consistent with the earlier class-level results: L recall improved, while I recall decreased. The attention mechanism appears to have shifted the decision behaviour between the two visually similar classes rather than producing a clear overall reduction in confusion.

7.15 Visual Inspection of Remaining I–L Errors¶

Misclassified I and L samples are displayed to see whether the remaining errors appear visually ambiguous.

This is a diagnostic analysis only. The images do not prove what the model is attending to.

In [32]:
def show_il_errors(y_true, y_pred, X_images, max_images=20, title="I–L Misclassifications"):
    mask = (
        ((y_true == I_INDEX) & (y_pred == L_INDEX)) |
        ((y_true == L_INDEX) & (y_pred == I_INDEX))
    )

    indices = np.where(mask)[0][:max_images]

    if len(indices) == 0:
        print("No I–L errors found.")
        return

    cols = 5
    rows = int(np.ceil(len(indices) / cols))

    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 2.2 * rows))

    for plot_idx, image_idx in enumerate(indices, start=1):
        plt.subplot(rows, cols, plot_idx)
        plt.imshow(X_images[image_idx].squeeze(), cmap="gray")

        true_letter = LETTERS[y_true[image_idx]]
        pred_letter = LETTERS[y_pred[image_idx]]

        plt.title(f"True: {true_letter} | Pred: {pred_letter}")
        plt.axis("off")

    plt.suptitle(title)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


show_il_errors(
    y_test_int,
    baseline_result["Predictions"],
    X_test,
    title="V2 Baseline — I–L Misclassifications"
)

show_il_errors(
    y_test_int,
    cbam_result["Predictions"],
    X_test,
    title="V2 + CBAM — I–L Misclassifications"
)

Visual Analysis of I–L Misclassifications¶

The misclassified I and L samples show that many errors occur on characters with extremely similar stroke structures.

Visual Characteristics¶

Several patterns are visible in both the V2 Baseline and V2 + CBAM errors:

  • many samples consist mainly of a single narrow vertical or slanted stroke;
  • some true L samples have a very short or weak lower horizontal stroke, making them resemble I;
  • some true I samples are slightly curved or slanted, making them resemble handwritten L;
  • the low 28×28 resolution further reduces small structural differences between the two letters.

In several examples, the visual distinction between I and L is difficult even for a human observer because the character contains very little discriminative information.

Comparison Between Models¶

The V2 Baseline and V2 + CBAM models misclassify many samples with similar visual characteristics.

This supports the numerical results showing that CBAM did not substantially reduce total I–L confusion. Instead, it changed the direction of the errors:

  • I→L errors increased from 62 to 95;
  • L→I errors decreased from 155 to 121;
  • total I↔L errors remained almost unchanged at 217 versus 216.

Interpretation¶

These examples suggest that the remaining I–L errors are not caused only by insufficient feature attention. Some samples contain inherently weak or ambiguous visual evidence for distinguishing the two classes.

CBAM can reweight important channel and spatial features, but it cannot create discriminative stroke information that is absent or barely visible in the original image.

Therefore, the qualitative results help explain why CBAM mainly redistributed the I–L errors rather than eliminating them.

8. Experiment 2 — V3 Augmentation with and without CBAM¶

8.1 Motivation¶

Experiment 1 showed that adding CBAM to V2 did not produce a clear overall improvement.

Although the V2 + CBAM model achieved a slightly lower test loss and improved the recognition of some difficult classes such as L, overall test accuracy and macro F1 decreased slightly. The total I–L confusion also remained almost unchanged, indicating that CBAM mainly redistributed the errors between I and L rather than resolving the confusion.

CA1 Part A found that V3, which retains the V2 architecture but trains using data augmentation, achieved stronger overall performance than V2. Therefore, a second controlled experiment is performed to determine whether CBAM behaves differently when combined with the stronger V3 training strategy.

This experiment investigates whether the additional variation introduced by data augmentation allows the attention mechanism to learn more useful and robust features than in the non-augmented V2 setting.

Hypothesis¶

Combining realistic data augmentation with CBAM may provide a stronger benefit than CBAM alone by exposing the network to greater variation in character orientation, position and scale.

However, because Experiment 1 did not show a consistent improvement from CBAM, this experiment also tests whether the attention mechanism remains beneficial when applied to an already stronger augmented model.

Controlled Comparison¶

The two models in this experiment are:

  • V3 Augmented: CA1 V2 architecture trained using the original CA1 V3 augmentation settings
  • V3 + CBAM: the same backbone and augmentation settings, with CBAM added after each convolutional block

Both models receive the same augmented training data and training configuration. Therefore, CBAM remains the main architectural difference between the two models.

8.2 Recreate the CA1 V3 Data Augmentation¶

The augmentation configuration is reproduced directly from CA1 Part A.

Transformation Setting Purpose
Rotation 5° Simulates small natural handwriting tilt
Zoom 0.1 Simulates small differences in character scale
Width shift 0.1 Simulates horizontal positioning differences
Height shift 0.1 Simulates vertical positioning differences
Horizontal flip False Prevents invalid mirrored characters
Fill mode nearest Fills pixels introduced by geometric transformations

The validation and test sets are not augmented. This ensures that both models are evaluated on the original unseen images.

In [33]:

    fill_mode="nearest"
)

datagen_v3_cbam = ImageDataGenerator(**AUGMENTATION_CONFIG)

8.4 Build the V3 Augmented Control Model¶

V3 uses the same CNN architecture as V2. Its improvement in CA1 came from training with augmented images rather than from changing the network structure.

Therefore, the V3 control model below reuses the same architecture as the V2 baseline. The difference appears later during training, where batches are generated by ImageDataGenerator.

In [35]:
def build_v3_baseline(input_shape=(28, 28, 1), num_classes=26):
    inputs = Input(shape=input_shape, name="input")

    x = Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation="relu", name="conv1")(inputs)
    x = BatchNormalization(name="bn1")(x)
    x = MaxPooling2D((2, 2), name="pool1")(x)

    x = Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation="relu", padding="same", name="conv2")(x)
    x = BatchNormalization(name="bn2")(x)
    x = MaxPooling2D((2, 2), name="pool2")(x)

    x = Conv2D(128, (3, 3), activation="relu", padding="same", name="conv3")(x)
    x = BatchNormalization(name="bn3")(x)

    x = Flatten(name="flatten")(x)
    x = Dense(256, activation="relu", name="dense256")(x)
    x = Dropout(0.4, name="dropout")(x)

    outputs = Dense(num_classes, activation="softmax", name="output")(x)

    return Model(inputs, outputs, name="CA1_V3_Augmented")


v3_model = build_v3_baseline()

v3_model.compile(
    loss="categorical_crossentropy",
    optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.0005),
    metrics=["accuracy"]
)

v3_model.summary()

8.5 Build the V3 + CBAM Model¶

Hypothesis

If CBAM and data augmentation provide complementary benefits, adding CBAM to V3 should improve feature selection while augmentation improves robustness to handwriting variation.

The V3 + CBAM model therefore keeps:

  • the V3/V2 convolutional backbone;
  • Batch Normalisation;
  • Dropout;
  • the original V3 augmentation settings;

and inserts a CBAM block after each convolutional feature block.

In [36]:
def build_v3_cbam(input_shape=(28, 28, 1), num_classes=26, reduction_ratio=8):
    inputs = Input(shape=input_shape, name="input")

    x = Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation="relu", name="conv1")(inputs)
    x = BatchNormalization(name="bn1")(x)
    x = cbam_block(x, reduction_ratio=reduction_ratio, name="cbam1")
    x = MaxPooling2D((2, 2), name="pool1")(x)

    x = Conv2D(64, (3, 3), activation="relu", padding="same", name="conv2")(x)
    x = BatchNormalization(name="bn2")(x)
    x = cbam_block(x, reduction_ratio=reduction_ratio, name="cbam2")
    x = MaxPooling2D((2, 2), name="pool2")(x)

    x = Conv2D(128, (3, 3), activation="relu", padding="same", name="conv3")(x)
    x = BatchNormalization(name="bn3")(x)
    x = cbam_block(x, reduction_ratio=reduction_ratio, name="cbam3")

    x = Flatten(name="flatten")(x)
    x = Dense(256, activation="relu", name="dense256")(x)
    x = Dropout(0.4, name="dropout")(x)

    outputs = Dense(num_classes, activation="softmax", name="output")(x)

    return Model(inputs, outputs, name="CA1_V3_CBAM")


v3_cbam_model = build_v3_cbam()

v3_cbam_model.compile(
    loss="categorical_crossentropy",
    optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.0005),
    metrics=["accuracy"]
)

v3_cbam_model.summary()

8.6 Parameter Comparison¶

The parameter count is compared before training to measure how much model size is added by CBAM.

Because V2 and V3 use the same underlying CNN architecture, the V3 control model should have the same parameter count as the V2 baseline. Any increase in the V3 + CBAM model is therefore caused by the attention modules.

In [37]:
v3_params = v3_model.count_params()
v3_cbam_params = v3_cbam_model.count_params()

v3_parameter_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Model": ["V3 Augmented", "V3 + CBAM"],
    "Parameters": [v3_params, v3_cbam_params]
})

display(v3_parameter_table)

v3_param_increase = v3_cbam_params - v3_params
v3_param_increase_pct = (v3_param_increase / v3_params) * 100

print(f"Additional parameters from CBAM: {v3_param_increase:,}")
print(f"Relative parameter increase: {v3_param_increase_pct:.3f}%")
Model Parameters
0 V3 Augmented 1280154
1 V3 + CBAM 1286076 
Additional parameters from CBAM: 5,922
Relative parameter increase: 0.463%

Parameter Comparison Analysis¶

Adding CBAM increased the parameter count from 1,280,154 to 1,286,076, which is only 5,922 additional parameters or approximately 0.463%.

This confirms that CBAM is lightweight in model size, even though its effect on training time and predictive performance must still be evaluated separately.

8.7 Training Setup¶

The original CA1 V3 training strategy is retained:

  • Adam optimiser;
  • learning rate = 0.0005;
  • batch size = 128;
  • maximum epochs = 20;
  • Early Stopping monitors validation loss;
  • patience = 3;
  • best validation weights are restored.

Both V3 models use the same augmentation configuration and the same seed.

This creates a fair comparison in which the main architectural difference is CBAM.

In [38]:
def make_v3_early_stopping():
    return EarlyStopping(
        monitor="val_loss",
        patience=3,
        restore_best_weights=True
    )

8.8 Train the V3 Augmented Model¶

This model acts as the control for Experiment 2.

It reproduces the CA1 V3 approach: the V2 architecture is trained on augmented batches while validation is performed on the original, unaugmented validation set.

In [39]:
reset_seed(SEED)

v3_model = build_v3_baseline()

v3_model.compile(
    loss="categorical_crossentropy",
    optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.0005),
    metrics=["accuracy"]
)

v3_start = time.time()

history_v3 = v3_model.fit(
    datagen_v3.flow(
        X_train,
        y_train,
        batch_size=128,
        shuffle=True,
        seed=SEED
    ),
    steps_per_epoch=len(X_train) // 128,
    validation_data=(X_val, y_val),
    epochs=20,
    callbacks=[make_v3_early_stopping()],
    verbose=1
)

v3_time = time.time() - v3_start

print(f"V3 training time: {v3_time:.2f} seconds")
print(f"V3 epochs completed: {len(history_v3.history['loss'])}")

8.10 Training History Comparison¶

Training and validation accuracy/loss are compared to determine:

  • whether both models converge;
  • whether CBAM improves validation performance;
  • whether either model shows signs of overfitting;
  • whether augmentation changes the training-validation gap.

The curves should be interpreted together with the final test-set results.

In [41]:
def plot_v3_history_comparison(history_a, history_b, metric="accuracy"):
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))

    plt.plot(history_a.history[metric], label="V3 Augmented Train")
    plt.plot(history_a.history[f"val_{metric}"], label="V3 Augmented Validation")
    plt.plot(history_b.history[metric], label="V3 + CBAM Train")
    plt.plot(history_b.history[f"val_{metric}"], label="V3 + CBAM Validation")

    plt.xlabel("Epoch")
    plt.ylabel(metric.title())
    plt.title(f"V3 vs V3 + CBAM — {metric.title()} Comparison")
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(alpha=0.3)
    plt.show()


plot_v3_history_comparison(history_v3, history_v3_cbam, metric="accuracy")
plot_v3_history_comparison(history_v3, history_v3_cbam, metric="loss")

Training-History Analysis¶

The training curves show that both models learned quickly during the first few epochs and then converged to similar accuracy and loss levels.

Accuracy¶

  • Both models reached above 90% validation accuracy after the first few epochs.
  • V3 Augmented continued to improve gradually and maintained validation accuracy around 93–94%.
  • V3 + CBAM showed a much lower initial validation accuracy, but recovered rapidly after the first epoch.
  • After convergence, the two models followed very similar accuracy trends, with no clear sustained advantage from CBAM.

Loss¶

  • Training and validation loss decreased sharply for both models during the early epochs.
  • V3 + CBAM started with a much higher validation loss, but this dropped quickly after the first epoch.
  • At later epochs, the loss curves became similar, although V3 Augmented generally maintained slightly better validation behaviour.
  • There is no strong sign of severe overfitting because the training and validation curves remain relatively close.

Overall Interpretation¶

The training history suggests that CBAM did not provide a clear optimisation or generalisation advantage when combined with V3 augmentation.

Although V3 + CBAM eventually converged to a similar training region, the final test results show that V3 Augmented achieved better accuracy, lower test loss and higher macro F1.

Therefore, the additional attention mechanism increased model complexity without producing a corresponding improvement in final performance.

8.11 Test-Set Evaluation¶

Evaluation Metrics

The same metrics used in Experiment 1 are retained:

  • test accuracy;
  • test loss;
  • macro F1;
  • I precision and recall;
  • L precision and recall;
  • I→L errors;
  • L→I errors;
  • total I↔L confusion;
  • parameter count;
  • training time.

Using the same evaluation function ensures that V2 and V3 experiments can be compared consistently.

)

V3 Test-Set Comparison Analysis¶

The V3 results show that adding CBAM did not improve the stronger augmented model.

Metric V3 Augmented V3 + CBAM Change

Key Observations¶

  • V3 Augmented achieved the stronger overall result, with higher test accuracy and macro F1 and lower test loss.
  • Adding CBAM reduced test accuracy by about 0.35 percentage points and increased test loss.
  • For I, precision improved but recall decreased substantially, resulting in 45 more I→L errors.
  • For L, recall improved substantially and L→I errors decreased by 39.
  • These class-specific changes again show a trade-off between I and L rather than a consistent improvement.
  • Total I↔L confusion increased from 220 to 226 errors, so CBAM did not improve the targeted confusion problem.
  • CBAM added only 0.46% more parameters, but the observed training time increased by approximately 34.6%.

Overall Interpretation¶

The V3 experiment provides stronger evidence that CBAM is not consistently beneficial for this task.

Although the attention mechanism improved certain class-specific metrics, particularly L recall, these gains were offset by weaker I recall and poorer overall generalisation.

The original V3 Augmented model remains the better configuration, suggesting that data augmentation provided a more effective improvement for EMNIST Letters than adding CBAM attention.

The classification reports show that V3 Augmented remained the stronger overall model, while adding CBAM produced mixed class-specific effects.

  • Q F1 therefore improved from 0.8807 to 0.8872.
  • CBAM again produced mixed class-specific effects rather than a consistent improvement across both members of the difficult pair.

Other Class-Level Changes¶

Several classes improved slightly after adding CBAM, including:

  • D: F1 increased from 0.9503 to 0.9577
  • O: 0.9706 → 0.9749
  • U: 0.9326 → 0.9372
  • A: 0.9371 → 0.9392

However, other classes decreased, including:

  • E: 0.9825 → 0.9675
  • Y: 0.9653 → 0.9519
  • R: 0.9657 → 0.9519
  • W: 0.9845 → 0.9759
  • B: 0.9755 → 0.9669

Overall Interpretation¶

The class-level results confirm that CBAM had a mixed and class-dependent effect when combined with V3 augmentation.

The clearest trade-off again occurred between I and L: L recall and F1 improved, while I recall and F1 decreased. For the secondary G–Q pair, Q improved slightly while G decreased slightly.

Despite some individual class improvements, these gains were not sufficient to improve the overall model. V3 Augmented retained higher accuracy and macro F1, showing that CBAM did not provide a consistent additional benefit when combined with data augmentation.

The research question specifically targets the persistent confusion between I and L.

The following chart compares both error directions separately because a reduction in I→L errors can occur at the same time as an increase in L→I errors.

I–L Confusion Analysis¶

The V3 comparison shows that adding CBAM again changed the direction of the I–L confusion, but did not reduce the overall problem.

Error Type V3 Augmented V3 + CBAM Change
I→L 103 148 +45
L→I 117 78 -39
Total I↔L 220 226 +6

Key Observations¶

  • I→L errors increased from 103 to 148, meaning that more true I samples were classified as L after adding CBAM.
  • L→I errors decreased from 117 to 78, showing improved recognition of L relative to I.
  • These directional changes are consistent with the class-level metrics: L recall improved, while I recall decreased.
  • Unlike Experiment 1, total I↔L confusion became slightly worse, increasing from 220 to 226 errors.

Interpretation¶

CBAM therefore did not resolve the I–L confusion in the augmented V3 setting.

Instead, it again shifted the decision behaviour between the two classes, favouring L more strongly while reducing recognition of I. The increase in total I–L errors further supports the finding that CBAM did not provide an additional benefit over V3 augmentation alone.

8.14 Visual Inspection of Remaining I–L Errors¶

Numerical metrics show how many errors remain, but they do not show why the samples are difficult.

The remaining I–L errors are therefore displayed to inspect whether the two classes are still visually ambiguous after combining augmentation with CBAM.

In [45]:
show_il_errors(
    y_test_int,
    v3_result["Predictions"],
    X_test,
    title="V3 Augmented — I–L Misclassifications"
)

show_il_errors(
    y_test_int,
    v3_cbam_result["Predictions"],
    X_test,
    title="V3 + CBAM — I–L Misclassifications"
)

Visual Analysis of V3 I–L Misclassifications¶

The misclassified examples from both V3 Augmented and V3 + CBAM show that many I and L samples remain visually ambiguous.

Visual Characteristics¶

  • Many samples are formed by only a single narrow vertical or slanted stroke.
  • Some true L samples have a very weak or short lower stroke, causing them to resemble I.
  • Some true I samples are curved or angled, making them resemble handwritten L.
  • At the low 28×28 resolution, these small structural differences can be difficult to distinguish.

Several examples are sufficiently ambiguous that even a human observer may find it difficult to confidently determine whether the character should be labelled I or L.

Comparison Between Models¶

The two models show similar types of difficult samples, but the direction of their errors differs.

  • V3 Augmented: I→L = 103, L→I = 117
  • V3 + CBAM: I→L = 148, L→I = 78

After adding CBAM, more I samples were classified as L, while fewer L samples were classified as I.

This agrees with the class-level results, where L recall improved but I recall decreased.

Interpretation¶

The visual examples suggest that the remaining confusion is partly caused by limited discriminative information in the input images, rather than simply insufficient model complexity.

CBAM can emphasise important channel and spatial features, but it cannot recover stroke information that is weak or absent in the original image.

This helps explain why CBAM changed the direction of the I–L errors without reducing the overall confusion, which increased slightly from 220 to 226 errors.

9.1 Final Four-Model Comparison Analysis¶

The final table combines both controlled experiments:

  1. V2 Baseline
  2. V2 + CBAM
  3. V3 Augmented
  4. V3 + CBAM

This makes it possible to distinguish the contribution of:

  • the original V2 architecture;
  • CBAM attention;
  • V3 data augmentation;
  • the combination of augmentation and CBAM.

The final model should be selected based on overall test performance, I–L behaviour and computational cost, rather than accuracy alone.

Final Four-Model Comparison Analysis¶

The four-model comparison shows that V3 Augmented achieved the strongest overall classification performance.

Model Test Accuracy (%) Test Loss Macro F1 Total I↔L Errors
V2 Baseline 93.9489 0.1929 0.9392 217
V2 + CBAM 93.7988 0.1922 0.9379 216
V3 Augmented 94.4294 0.1552 0.9443 220
V3 + CBAM 94.0766 0.1698 0.9405 226

Overall Performance¶

  • V3 Augmented achieved the highest test accuracy at 94.43%, the lowest test loss at 0.1552, and the highest macro F1 at 0.9443.
  • V3 therefore provided a clear overall improvement over the V2 Baseline.
  • Adding CBAM did not improve overall performance for either backbone.
  • V2 + CBAM decreased accuracy slightly from 93.95% to 93.80%.
  • V3 + CBAM decreased accuracy from 94.43% to 94.08%.

I–L Confusion¶

The I–L results show a different pattern from the overall metrics.

  • V2 + CBAM achieved the lowest total I↔L confusion, with 216 errors, compared with 217 for V2 Baseline.
  • However, this reduction was only one error, so it does not represent a meaningful overall improvement.
  • V3 Augmented produced 220 I↔L errors despite achieving the best overall classification performance.
  • Adding CBAM to V3 increased the targeted confusion further to 226 errors.

Across both experiments, CBAM mainly changed the direction of I–L errors. It tended to improve L recall while reducing I recall, rather than improving both classes simultaneously.

Data Augmentation versus CBAM¶

The comparison suggests that data augmentation was more effective than CBAM attention for this EMNIST Letters task.

Moving from V2 Baseline to V3 Augmented:

  • accuracy increased from 93.95% to 94.43%;
  • test loss decreased from 0.1929 to 0.1552;
  • macro F1 increased from 0.9392 to 0.9443.

In contrast, adding CBAM to either V2 or V3 did not improve the overall test metrics.

This indicates that exposing the CNN to realistic variations in rotation, position and scale provided a more useful generalisation benefit than adding channel-spatial attention.

Computational Trade-off¶

CBAM increased the parameter count by only approximately 0.46%, confirming that it is lightweight in terms of model size.

However, the observed training times increased considerably:

  • V2: 158.80 s → 365.73 s
  • V3: 342.31 s → 460.91 s

Therefore, the small increase in parameter count did not translate into an equally small training-time overhead.

Overall Interpretation¶

The complete experiment does not support the hypothesis that CBAM consistently improves the CA1 CNN for EMNIST Letters.

Instead, the results show that:

  • V3 Augmented is the strongest overall model;
  • CBAM produces mixed, class-dependent changes;
  • CBAM does not substantially resolve the difficult I–L confusion;
  • data augmentation provides a more effective improvement than attention for this task;
  • additional architectural complexity does not automatically lead to better generalisation.

The main finding is therefore that the effectiveness of CBAM is context-dependent. Although it can alter how the network prioritises features and change class-specific behaviour, it did not provide a consistent advantage over the original CNN configurations in these experiments.

Key Finding¶

Across both V2 and V3, adding CBAM consistently reduced L→I errors but increased I→L errors.

Therefore, CBAM mainly changed the direction of the I–L confusion rather than reducing the total problem.

V2 + CBAM achieved the lowest total I↔L error count at 216, but this was only one fewer error than the V2 Baseline. Meanwhile, V3 Augmented remained the strongest model overall despite not achieving the lowest I–L confusion count.

9.3 Multi-Seed Robustness Check (V2 and V3, CBAM vs No-CBAM)¶

All four models above were trained using a single random seed (SEED = 88). Small differences in test accuracy, macro F1 and I–L error counts could therefore be partly explained by training-run variation (random weight initialisation and batch shuffling) rather than a genuine effect of CBAM.

To check this, the four models are retrained across three seeds while keeping the train/validation/test split fixed (the same split used everywhere else in this notebook). Only the model's weight initialisation and training-batch shuffling change between seeds — this isolates training-run variance and lets us report whether CBAM's effect (in particular the I→L / L→I error redistribution) is consistent across runs, or specific to seed 88.

Note: this retrains 4 models × 3 seeds = 12 models from scratch. On a GPU this typically takes 30–90 minutes; on CPU it will be much longer.

In [48]:
MULTISEED_SEEDS = [42, 88, 123]   # 88 is kept so one run matches Sections 7-9 above
multiseed_records = []

for seed in MULTISEED_SEEDS:

    # ---- V2 Baseline ----
    reset_seed(seed)
    m = build_v2_baseline()
    m.compile(loss="categorical_crossentropy", optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.0005), metrics=["accuracy"])
    t0 = time.time()
    m.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val),
          epochs=20, batch_size=128, callbacks=[make_early_stopping()],
          verbose=0, shuffle=True)
    r = evaluate_model(m, "V2 Baseline", time.time() - t0)
    r["Seed"] = seed
    multiseed_records.append(r)
    print(f"Seed {seed} | V2 Baseline — Acc {r['Test Accuracy (%)']:.2f}%, I↔L {r['Total I↔L Errors']}")

    # ---- V2 + CBAM ----
    reset_seed(seed)
    m = build_v2_cbam()
    m.compile(loss="categorical_crossentropy", optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.0005), metrics=["accuracy"])
    t0 = time.time()
    m.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val),
          epochs=20, batch_size=128, callbacks=[make_early_stopping()],
          verbose=0, shuffle=True)
    r = evaluate_model(m, "V2 + CBAM", time.time() - t0)
    r["Seed"] = seed
    multiseed_records.append(r)
    print(f"Seed {seed} | V2 + CBAM — Acc {r['Test Accuracy (%)']:.2f}%, I↔L {r['Total I↔L Errors']}")

    # ---- V3 Augmented ----
    reset_seed(seed)
    m = build_v3_baseline()
    m.compile(loss="categorical_crossentropy", optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.0005), metrics=["accuracy"])
    datagen = ImageDataGenerator(**AUGMENTATION_CONFIG)
    t0 = time.time()
    m.fit(datagen.flow(X_train, y_train, batch_size=128, shuffle=True, seed=seed),
          steps_per_epoch=len(X_train) // 128,
          validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=20,
          callbacks=[make_v3_early_stopping()], verbose=0)
    r = evaluate_model(m, "V3 Augmented", time.time() - t0)
    r["Seed"] = seed
    multiseed_records.append(r)
    print(f"Seed {seed} | V3 Augmented — Acc {r['Test Accuracy (%)']:.2f}%, I↔L {r['Total I↔L Errors']}")

    # ---- V3 + CBAM ----
    reset_seed(seed)
    m = build_v3_cbam()
    m.compile(loss="categorical_crossentropy", optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.0005), metrics=["accuracy"])
    datagen = ImageDataGenerator(**AUGMENTATION_CONFIG)
    t0 = time.time()
    m.fit(datagen.flow(X_train, y_train, batch_size=128, shuffle=True, seed=seed),
          steps_per_epoch=len(X_train) // 128,
          validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=20,
          callbacks=[make_v3_early_stopping()], verbose=0)
    r = evaluate_model(m, "V3 + CBAM", time.time() - t0)
    r["Seed"] = seed
    multiseed_records.append(r)
    print(f"Seed {seed} | V3 + CBAM — Acc {r['Test Accuracy (%)']:.2f}%, I↔L {r['Total I↔L Errors']}")

9.4 Multi-Seed Robustness Interpretation¶

The single-seed results above (Sections 7–9) came from one training run per model (SEED = 88). Retraining across three seeds (42, 88, 123) on the same train/val/test split tests whether the CBAM effect is a genuine pattern or an artefact of one run.

Metric V2 Baseline V2 + CBAM V3 Augmented V3 + CBAM
Test Accuracy (%) 93.89 ± 0.08 93.88 ± 0.30 94.48 ± 0.23 94.28 ± 0.24
Test Loss 0.195 ± 0.002 0.186 ± 0.008 0.159 ± 0.004 0.166 ± 0.003
Macro F1 0.939 ± 0.001 0.939 ± 0.003 0.945 ± 0.002 0.943 ± 0.003
I→L Errors 85.3 ± 22.5 100.0 ± 15.1 115.7 ± 23.7 124.3 ± 28.3
L→I Errors 134.0 ± 24.6 119.7 ± 8.1 103.3 ± 19.5 95.7 ± 24.8
Total I↔L Errors 219.3 ± 6.8 219.7 ± 7.2 219.0 ± 5.6 220.0 ± 5.2

Key findings

  • Total I↔L errors barely move. Across all four models and all three seeds, total I↔L confusion stays in a narrow ~219–220 band regardless of CBAM. The "redistribution, not reduction" finding from Section 10.1/10.2 is not specific to seed 88.
  • Overall accuracy/macro F1 gap is not meaningful. The V2 accuracy gap (−0.01 pp) is far smaller than the seed-to-seed spread; the V3 gap (−0.20 pp) is roughly the same size as its spread rather than clearly exceeding it.
  • V2's directional effect is fully consistent: I→L errors rose with CBAM in every seed (87→88, 62→95, 107→117). L→I fell in 2 of 3 seeds and was flat in the third.
  • V3's directional effect is less stable: the same I→L-up/L→I-down pattern held at seeds 42 and 88, but reversed at seed 123 (I→L: 143→93, L→I: 81→124). A single-seed comparison could not have revealed this.

This means the CBAM finding is robust for V2, but the V3+CBAM interaction appears more sensitive to training randomness than a single run suggested.

10. Discussion and Failure-Case Analysis¶

The two controlled experiments show that adding CBAM did not provide a consistent improvement to the EMNIST Letters classifiers.

Although CBAM is designed to emphasise informative channels and spatial regions, its effect in this task was mixed. The attention mechanism changed how the models classified difficult letters, particularly I and L, but these class-specific changes did not translate into better overall generalisation.

10.1 Experiment 1 — V2 Baseline vs V2 + CBAM¶

The first experiment isolated the architectural effect of CBAM by comparing the V2 Baseline with the same CNN enhanced using CBAM.

Metric V2 Baseline V2 + CBAM Change
Test Accuracy (%) 93.9489 93.7988 −0.1501 pp
Test Loss 0.1929 0.1922 −0.0007
Macro F1 0.9392 0.9379 −0.0013
I→L Errors 62 95 +33
L→I Errors 155 121 −34
Total I↔L Errors 217 216 −1

Key Findings

  • Adding CBAM slightly reduced test accuracy and macro F1.
  • Test loss improved only marginally.
  • Total I↔L confusion decreased by only one error, from 217 to 216.
  • However, the direction of the errors changed substantially:
    • I→L errors increased from 62 to 95;
    • L→I errors decreased from 155 to 121.
  • This is consistent with the class-level metrics, where recognition of L improved, while recognition of I became weaker.

Therefore, CBAM did not meaningfully solve the I–L confusion in Experiment 1. Instead, it mainly redistributed the errors between the two classes.

This result also shows why total error count alone is insufficient. Although the total number of I↔L errors decreased by one, this hides a large shift in which class was being misclassified.

10.2 Experiment 2 — V3 Augmented vs V3 + CBAM¶

The second experiment tested whether CBAM became more useful when combined with the stronger V3 data-augmentation strategy.

Both models used the same augmentation pipeline, meaning that CBAM remained the main architectural difference.

Metric V3 Augmented V3 + CBAM Change
Test Accuracy (%) 94.4294 94.0766 −0.3528 pp
Test Loss 0.1552 0.1698 +0.0146
Macro F1 0.9443 0.9405 −0.0038
I→L Errors 103 148 +45
L→I Errors 117 78 −39
Total I↔L Errors 220 226 +6

Key Findings

  • V3 Augmented achieved higher test accuracy and macro F1 and lower test loss.
  • Adding CBAM reduced test accuracy by approximately 0.35 percentage points.
  • I→L errors increased by 45, from 103 to 148.
  • L→I errors decreased by 39, from 117 to 78.
  • Total I↔L confusion increased from 220 to 226 errors.
  • The same directional trade-off observed in Experiment 1 therefore appeared again: CBAM improved recognition of L while weakening recognition of I.

The second experiment provides stronger evidence that CBAM was not beneficial overall for this task.

Data augmentation and attention were expected to provide potentially complementary improvements, but the results did not support this hypothesis. The original V3 Augmented model remained stronger than V3 + CBAM.

10.3 Data Augmentation vs CBAM¶

The final four-model comparison shows that V3 Augmented achieved the strongest overall classification performance.

Model Test Accuracy (%) Test Loss Macro F1 Total I↔L Errors
V2 Baseline 93.9489 0.1929 0.9392 217
V2 + CBAM 93.7988 0.1922 0.9379 216
V3 Augmented 94.4294 0.1552 0.9443 220
V3 + CBAM 94.0766 0.1698 0.9405 226

Moving from V2 Baseline to V3 Augmented improved:

  • test accuracy from 93.95% to 94.43%;
  • test loss from 0.1929 to 0.1552; and
  • macro F1 from 0.9392 to 0.9443.

In contrast, adding CBAM to either V2 or V3 did not improve overall test performance.

This suggests that, for this dataset, exposing the CNN to realistic variation in character position, rotation and scale provided a more useful generalisation benefit than adding channel-spatial attention.

The result also demonstrates that a more advanced architecture does not automatically produce a better model. The usefulness of an architectural component depends on the task, data and existing baseline strength.

10.4 Computational Trade-off¶

CBAM remained lightweight in terms of parameter count.

The V2/V3 CNN contains 1,280,154 parameters, while the CBAM-enhanced version contains 1,286,076 parameters.

This is an increase of only:

[ 5,922 \text{ parameters} \approx 0.46% ]

However, the observed training time increased substantially:

Experiment Without CBAM With CBAM
V2 158.80 s 365.73 s
V3 342.31 s 460.91 s

For V3, CBAM increased the observed training time by approximately 34.6%.

Training time is influenced by both the computational cost of the model and the number of epochs completed before Early Stopping, so these values should not be interpreted as pure per-step computational overhead.

Nevertheless, within these experiments, the additional training cost did not produce a corresponding improvement in final classification performance.

10.5 Failure-Case Analysis¶

The remaining I–L misclassifications provide an important explanation for why CBAM did not substantially solve the targeted confusion problem.

Observed Failure Patterns

The visual inspection showed several repeated characteristics:

  • many difficult samples consist mainly of a single narrow vertical or slanted stroke;
  • some true L samples contain only a very short or weak lower horizontal stroke, causing them to resemble I;
  • some true I samples are curved or slanted, making them resemble handwritten L;
  • at the low 28×28 resolution, small distinguishing stroke details may occupy only a few pixels; and
  • several samples are sufficiently ambiguous that even a human observer may find them difficult to classify confidently.

These failure cases suggest that the remaining confusion is not caused only by insufficient feature attention.

CBAM can change the importance assigned to existing channel and spatial features, but it cannot recover discriminative information that is weak or absent in the original input.

This helps explain why CBAM changed the direction of the I–L errors without consistently reducing their total number.

10.6 What Worked, What Did Not, and What Was Learnt¶

Finding Outcome
Data augmentation Worked — V3 achieved the strongest overall accuracy, loss and macro F1
CBAM on V2 Did not improve overall performance — only a very small loss improvement and one fewer I↔L error
CBAM on V3 Did not improve performance — accuracy, loss, macro F1 and total I↔L confusion became worse
L recognition with CBAM Improved — L→I errors decreased in both experiments
I recognition with CBAM Worsened — I→L errors increased in both experiments
Failure-case inspection Useful — showed that many remaining errors contain very weak visual differences

The most important lesson from the experiment is that adding a more advanced attention mechanism does not guarantee better generalisation.

CBAM produced measurable changes in model behaviour, but the changes were class-dependent rather than consistently beneficial.

The negative result is still informative because it identifies both what the attention mechanism changed and why those changes were insufficient to outperform the simpler V3 Augmented model. Section 9.4 confirms this pattern is not specific to this one run: across three seeds, the V2 redistribution effect was fully consistent, while the V3 effect held in two of three seeds but reversed at the third — so the story above generalises well for V2 and only partially for V3.

11. Conclusion and Further Improvements¶

11.1 Research Question 1¶

To what extent does integrating CBAM improve CNN-based EMNIST Letters classification, particularly for the visually ambiguous I and L classes?

Answer

The first research question is answered negatively overall, with class-specific effects.

For the V2 experiment, adding CBAM:

  • decreased test accuracy from 93.95% to 93.80%;
  • decreased macro F1 from 0.9392 to 0.9379;
  • improved test loss only marginally from 0.1929 to 0.1922; and
  • reduced total I↔L confusion by only one error, from 217 to 216.

However, the direction of the I–L errors changed substantially:

  • I→L errors increased from 62 to 95;
  • L→I errors decreased from 155 to 121.

Therefore, CBAM did not meaningfully resolve the I–L confusion. Instead, it mainly shifted the decision behaviour between the two visually similar classes. This was confirmed across three seeds (Section 9.4): I→L errors rose with CBAM in every seed tested, and total I↔L confusion stayed within a narrow band regardless of CBAM.

11.2 Research Question 2¶

Does CBAM remain beneficial when combined with the stronger CA1 V3 data-augmentation strategy?

Answer

The second research question is answered no.

The V3 Augmented model achieved:

  • 94.43% test accuracy;
  • 0.1552 test loss; and
  • 0.9443 macro F1.

After adding CBAM:

  • accuracy decreased to 94.08%;
  • test loss increased to 0.1698;
  • macro F1 decreased to 0.9405; and
  • total I↔L confusion increased from 220 to 226 errors.

CBAM again improved L recognition while reducing I recognition, showing the same class-specific trade-off observed in Experiment 1.

Therefore, CBAM did not provide an additional benefit when combined with V3 augmentation. Across three seeds this direction held on average but was less consistent than Experiment 1, reversing at one seed — indicating the V3+CBAM interaction is more sensitive to training randomness than V2+CBAM.

11.3 Overall Finding¶

Across both experiments, CBAM produced a mixed and class-dependent effect, but it did not provide a consistent improvement in overall EMNIST Letters classification.

The strongest model was V3 Augmented, which achieved:

Metric Result
Test Accuracy 94.43%
Test Loss 0.1552
Macro F1 0.9443

The experiments therefore suggest that data augmentation was more effective than CBAM attention for this task.

CBAM remained lightweight in parameter count, adding only approximately 0.46% more parameters, but the observed training time increased without a corresponding improvement in final model performance.

The failure-case analysis also showed that many remaining I–L errors contain extremely weak or ambiguous distinguishing strokes. This suggests that the problem cannot necessarily be solved simply by increasing feature attention.

The main conclusion is therefore that a more advanced architectural component should be evaluated empirically rather than assumed to improve an already strong model.

Among the tested configurations, V3 Augmented is selected as the strongest overall model.

11.4 Limitations¶

The results should be interpreted with several limitations:

  • Only three random seeds: Section 9.4 confirmed the redistribution pattern across seeds 42, 88 and 123, but three seeds is still too few for formal statistical significance testing, particularly for the noisier V3 comparison.
  • Single CBAM configuration: Only one main CBAM design was evaluated.
  • Fixed CBAM placement: The attention modules were inserted at fixed locations rather than systematically comparing different placements.
  • Limited CBAM hyperparameter tuning: The channel reduction ratio and spatial kernel size were not extensively tuned.
  • Low image resolution: EMNIST images are only 28×28, limiting the amount of fine stroke information available.
  • Ambiguous handwriting: Some I and L samples contain weak or absent distinguishing strokes and may be difficult even for a human observer to classify confidently.
  • Training-time comparison: Observed training time is affected by both model computation and the number of epochs completed before Early Stopping.

These limitations mean that the results should not be interpreted as evidence that CBAM is ineffective in general. They show only that the tested CBAM configuration did not provide a consistent advantage for this specific EMNIST Letters setup.

11.5 Further Improvements¶

Future work could:

  • extend the multi-seed check (Section 9.4) to five or more seeds, especially for the V3 comparison, where the CBAM effect reversed at one of the three seeds already tested;
  • compare channel-only attention, spatial-only attention and full CBAM to identify which component causes the observed class-specific behaviour;
  • test different CBAM placements within the CNN;
  • tune the channel reduction ratio and spatial kernel size;
  • compare CBAM with other lightweight attention mechanisms such as Squeeze-and-Excitation;
  • use Grad-CAM or attention-map visualisation to investigate which stroke regions influence predictions;
  • investigate whether higher-resolution or alternative handwritten-character datasets provide enough visual detail for attention to be more beneficial; and
  • perform targeted analysis of other commonly confused letter pairs rather than focusing only on I and L.

11.6 Final Insight¶

This investigation demonstrates the value of reporting both successful and unsuccessful experiments.

The original expectation was that CBAM might help the CNN focus on subtle structural differences between visually similar handwritten letters. The results did not support this expectation.

Instead, the experiments showed that:

  • data augmentation provided the strongest overall improvement;
  • CBAM changed class-specific behaviour without improving overall generalisation;
  • improvements for one class can occur at the expense of another;
  • model complexity alone is not sufficient to guarantee better performance; and
  • visual failure-case analysis can reveal limitations that are not visible from accuracy alone.

Therefore, the main value of the experiment is not that CBAM produced a better model, but that the controlled comparisons explain when the proposed improvement failed, how model behaviour changed, and what could be investigated next.
